passage:
Tuesday
At dinner I said maybe I want commerce, not science. Appa didn't even look up. 'You'll understand when you're older.' Amma nodded. That's it. That's what they say about everything: my haircut, my friends, even debate club. So I've stopped telling them things. I didn't mention I got selected for the district debate. I told Amma the practice sessions were extra maths.
Tonight Vidya Akka found the certificate in my bag and asked why I'm hiding it. I said, 'What's the point? I'll understand when I'm older.' She didn't argue. She said she used to do the same, and it made everything worse later. I don't know. I just want one conversation where they actually listen.
Jeevan

qa.q: What did Vidya Akka find in Jeevan's bag?
qa.a: The district debate certificate.

qa.q: What does Jeevan feel about hearing 'You'll understand when you're older'?
qa.a: Jeevan feels unheard and frustrated, as if every opinion gets shut down, which has led to hiding things.

qa.q: What could help rebuild trust in this family?
qa.a: Jeevan could share the debate news with Vidya Akka's support, and Appa and Amma could ask about the commerce idea and truly listen instead of closing it.

qa.q: How might Vidya Akka see Jeevan's hiding?
qa.a: Vidya Akka recognises the pattern and seems worried, because hiding things once made life harder for her too.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose opinions are shut down with 'you'll understand when you're older', who goes quiet and hides things, harming trust on both sides.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,

You asked why I sound so quiet on calls. Here's the thing.

Every time I say what I think at home, Dad says, "You'll understand when you're older." About the arts stream. About the drama club. Even about which cricket team is better, which is ridiculous.

So I've stopped saying things. I joined the drama club anyway. I tell them it's extra maths on Thursdays. I hate that. I'd never lied to them before, and now there's this whole Thursday that doesn't exist.

Last night Mum asked why I never talk at dinner anymore. I said I was tired.

I think they think I'm growing up. I think I'm just hiding.

Don't tell your mum any of this; she'll tell mine.

Joseph

qa.q: What does Joseph tell the family about Thursdays?
qa.a: Joseph tells them it's extra maths on Thursdays.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about the Thursday cover story?
qa.a: Joseph feels guilty and unhappy about lying for the first time, and unheard at home, which is why the talking has stopped.

qa.q: What could Joseph try instead of hiding the drama club?
qa.a: Pick a calm moment, maybe with Mum first, say how 'you'll understand when you're older' shuts the talk down, and then tell the truth about Thursdays.

qa.q: How might Dad feel if he learned about the drama club this way?
qa.a: Dad would likely feel hurt and shut out, and might realise his phrase pushed Joseph into hiding.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose opinions are shut down with 'you'll understand when you're older', and who goes quiet and starts hiding things, harming trust both ways.

passage:
You asked when I stopped talking at family meetings. I can tell you the exact day. I'm Charu, by the way, Class 11.

We were deciding whether to sell Dadi's old house in Indore. I spent every summer of my life in that house. I said, "Can we at least keep the garden part?" And Vandana Bua said, "Beta, respect your elders. You'll understand when you're older." Everyone nodded and moved on.

It wasn't even a no. It was like I hadn't spoken.

After that I just didn't. When they asked my opinion on anything, I said, "Whatever you think." I started going out on Sundays so I'd miss the family calls.

Last week Bua phoned me herself. She said, "You've gone so quiet. Did I do something?" And I didn't know what to say, because the true answer was yes.

qa.q: Which part of the house did Charu want to keep?
qa.a: Charu asked to at least keep the garden part.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when Bua said 'You'll understand when you're older'?
qa.a: Charu felt unheard and dismissed, as if the words had never been spoken, which hurt more than a plain no.

qa.q: What could Charu say to Bua now?
qa.a: Tell her honestly and politely that the remark about the house felt dismissive, and ask to be heard in the next family decision.

qa.q: How might Bua be feeling when she phones?
qa.a: Bua seems worried and puzzled by the silence, sensing she may have hurt Charu without knowing how.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose opinion is silenced in the name of respect, who then goes quiet and avoids the family, harming trust on both sides.

passage:
Monday: At dinner Varun said the new colony parking rule was unfair to the guards. Papa waved his fork. "You'll understand when you're older. Eat." Varun ate.

Thursday: The class teacher kept Varun back for arguing in class. At home he told only his brother Eshaan. "Don't tell Papa. He'll just say I'm a child."

Two weeks later: The teacher phoned Papa. Papa came to Varun's door, phone still in hand. "Why did I hear this from her and not from you?"

Varun shrugged. "You'd have said I'll understand when I'm older."

Papa stood there a long moment. Then he sat on the bed. "Okay. Tell me about the parking rule."

qa.q: What did Varun think about the new colony parking rule?
qa.a: Varun said the new colony parking rule was unfair to the guards.

qa.q: Why did Varun tell only Eshaan about being kept back?
qa.a: Varun felt unheard and expected to be dismissed as a child, so he hid it from Papa.

qa.q: What did Papa's last step get right?
qa.a: Sitting down and asking about the parking rule showed he was willing to listen, which is how trust can start to come back.

qa.q: How did Papa feel hearing the news from the teacher first?
qa.a: Papa felt hurt and shut out; his question at the door showed trust had broken on his side too.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose opinions are shut down as childish, who then hides things from a parent, harming trust both ways until the parent listens.

passage:
Alka, you think Papa doesn't listen? Let your Jahnavi bua tell you about my own father. When I was fifteen, in Kanpur, every time I gave an opinion at the table, about college, about friends, even about the news, he'd say, "You'll understand when you're older. Eat your food." After a while I stopped talking. I went quiet at dinner, and I started hiding things. I joined the school debate team and told him it was extra maths class. I even won a trophy and hid it with a friend. It felt like freedom, and also like lying every day.
Then my mother found the trophy. My father was so hurt that I hadn't told him. I was so angry he'd never listened. We didn't talk properly for a year. Later he told me, "I thought silence was respect." Beta, that year cost us both.

qa.q: Where did young Jahnavi hide her trophy?
qa.a: With a friend.

qa.q: How did young Jahnavi feel when her father kept saying "You'll understand when you're older"?
qa.a: She felt unheard and shut down, which made her go quiet and start hiding things.

qa.q: What turning point in the story might have gone differently, and how?
qa.a: When the trophy was found; if her father had asked her opinion earlier, or she had told him about debate, they might not have lost a year of trust.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi's father feel when the trophy was found?
qa.a: He felt hurt that his daughter hadn't told him, and later admitted he thought silence was respect.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager whose opinions are shut down in the name of respect, who goes quiet and hides things, harming trust both ways.
